Griot de Porc

Served at: Fete de Papa Zaka - Feast of the Farmer Loa

Serves 6-8Prep 30 min (plus 4 hours to overnight marinating)Cook 1 hour 30 min

Griot de Porc, a beloved staple of Haitian cuisine, features succulent pork pieces marinated in citrus and spices, then simmered until tender before being fried to a crispy perfection. This hearty and flavorful dish is a perfect centerpiece for the Fete de Papa Zaka, honoring the Lwa of agriculture and farmers, symbolizing abundance and communal celebration during harvest time.

Ingredients

  • 3 pounds (1.4 kg) boneless pork shoulder (pork butt), cut into 1 1/2-inch (4 cm) cubes
  • 1/2 cup (120 ml) sour orange juice (or a mix of 1/4 cup lime juice and 1/4 cup orange juice)
  • 1/4 cup (60 ml) white vinegar
  • 6 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 Scotch bonnet pepper, stemmed and left whole (or finely minced for more heat, optional)
  • 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves, or 1 teaspoon dried thyme
  • 1 teaspoon whole cloves
  • 1 teaspoon salt, or to taste
  • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, or to taste
  • 2 cups (480 ml) water, plus more if needed
  • 3-4 cups (720-960 ml) vegetable oil, for frying

Method

  1. Place the pork cubes in a large bowl. Add the sour orange juice and white vinegar, tossing to coat. Let sit for 10 minutes, then drain thoroughly and rinse the pork under cold water. This step helps to clean the pork and remove any gamey odor.
  2. Return the rinsed pork to the bowl. Add the minced garlic, whole Scotch bonnet pepper (if using whole), thyme, whole cloves, salt, and black pepper. Mix well to ensure all pork pieces are coated.
  3. Cover the bowl and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or preferably overnight, allowing the flavors to meld.
  4. Transfer the marinated pork and all its marinade to a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven. Add 2 cups (480 ml) of water.
  5. Bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for 1 to 1.5 hours, or until the pork is very tender and easily pierced with a fork. The liquid should mostly evaporate, leaving the pork cooking in its rendered fat and a concentrated sauce. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
  6. Once the pork is tender and the liquid has reduced, remove the Scotch bonnet pepper if it was added whole. Increase the heat to medium-high and continue cooking, stirring frequently, until any remaining liquid has evaporated and the pork begins to brown in its own rendered fat.
  7. In a separate large, heavy-bottomed pot or deep skillet, heat the vegetable oil to 350°F (175°C).
  8. Carefully transfer the browned pork pieces (without too much of the rendered fat from the simmering pot) into the hot oil, working in batches if necessary to avoid overcrowding the pan.
  9. Fry the pork for 5-8 minutes, or until deeply golden brown and crispy on all sides.
  10. Using a slotted spoon, remove the fried griot from the oil and place it on a plate lined with paper towels to drain excess oil.
  11. Serve hot, traditionally with pikliz (spicy pickled cabbage slaw), fried plantains, and riz collé (rice and beans).

Tips

  • For authentic flavor, seek out sour oranges (bitter oranges). If unavailable, a 50/50 mix of fresh lime juice and regular orange juice is a good substitute.
  • Do not overcrowd the pan when frying; this ensures the pork gets crispy rather than steaming. Fry in batches if needed.
  • The Scotch bonnet pepper adds essential flavor. If you prefer less heat, leave it whole and remove it before frying; for more heat, you can prick it or mince it.
